en: Because these difficulties involve determining the faults through the theory of inference (*anumāna*) and are capable of refuting that [position], one must further ask with certainty:
In your statement that it is not the word "pure land" itself that is being manifested, do you mean that the wisdom of the pure land is being cited, or the essence of the pure land?
If one does not cite [the source], yet claims to cite it, this contradicts one's own school, for this teaching on the Pure Land is precisely what reveals the Pure Land.
If one does not cite it, there is no contradiction with other schools, as words that do not reveal it cannot be said to clarify the Pure Land.
Between these two considerations, if one examines the intent of the former [position], then—
This incurs the fallacy of contradicting one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
If they attempt to defend themselves by saying, "This [text] suddenly mentions the essence of the Pure Land and then states that one does not enter the Pure Land;

therefore, there is no fallacy of contradicting one's own words," then by this very same "suddenness," the reason becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, in either case—whether advancing or retreating—the argument is untenable.
Principle. Regarding the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the eight assertions and four divisions establish inference (*anumāna*) by refuting the three-part [theory], stating:

"Self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) must necessarily exist as the very essence of the capacity to cognize, because it is subsumed under the mental division (*cittabhāga*), just like the object-division (*nimittabhāga*). [Objection: Self-cognition should not be mind.

[The opponent] argues that [the probans] is subsumed under the category of "part" (*bhāga*), because there is no capacity for realization within the very essence [of the subject], just like a hare's horn and so forth.
He judges these two types of inference to be fallacious and not authentic, as both fail to avoid the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

That is to say: as for the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), since it is subsumed under the mental aspect (*cittabhāga*) just like the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*), it possesses the capacity to cognize its own substance.

However, as for [the self-cognizing aspect] being like the characteristic of the arising of visual consciousness, since it is subsumed under the mental aspect, it lacks the capacity to cognize its own substance.
Thus, the aforementioned reason suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, as for the self-cognizing aspect, it is like a rabbit...
Because the "aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the "non-existent" (*abhāva*) are identical in essence and capable of being cognized, it is not subsumed under the category of the mind.
[The opponent argues: "Just as the three aspects of the ear-consciousness are not separate from its essence and are thus subsumed under the category of the mind, so too is this case.
Thus, the latter reason is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If the opponent were to offer this defense: "The three aspects of the five consciousnesses are not separate from their essence..."
Therefore, it is also illogical for this [self-cognition] to be the object-condition (*ālambana*) of its own self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*).

This is because the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is inseparable from the three aspects (*trilakṣaṇa*), and the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the five consciousnesses is likewise capable of taking [it] as an object. If this is not admitted, how could that [self-cognition] be so?

Even if one were to admit the former [the object of self-cognition], one must certainly not admit this [that the five consciousnesses take it as an object]; for the five consciousnesses are indeed able to take it as an object.
In all locations within the dharma-realm, the characteristics of phenomena are intermingled; this contradicts both reason and scripture.
Precisely because these three aspects of the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) exist, they suffice to render those two reasons inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Even if one were to offer the defense that the three aspects of the objective part are not subsumed under the category of mind, there would still be the fault of contradicting inference (*anumāna-virodha*). It should be understood as follows:
The fourth section of the *Jñānaprasthāna* states that there are words without corresponding reality.

Regarding the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* subsumes nine categories under the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). To establish the eighth category, it sets forth two syllogisms (*prayoga*) in opposition to the Hīnayāna.
This means that the teaching of the eight consciousnesses is subsumed under the authoritative words of the Sage because it resembles the absence of self, just like the four Āgamas.
Furthermore, the teaching of the eight consciousnesses accords with reason because it is the teaching of the Sage, just like the teaching of the six consciousnesses.

Thus, through this successive reasoning, it is established that there are eight consciousnesses. Now, within this context, we shall directly establish a formal inference (*anumāna*) based on the expressed meaning:

the visual, auditory, and olfactory consciousnesses must necessarily possess other distinct consciousnesses not subsumed under the gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousnesses, because they are not subsumed under any of the three [remaining] consciousnesses among the six sense-gates, just like the gustatory and tactile consciousnesses.

[This refers to] the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). In this context, the six consciousnesses are established for others as the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), while the eight consciousnesses are accepted by ourselves as our own dissimilar class;
thus, the inclusion of the cause within those three [consciousnesses] does not apply to them. Therefore, this reason is certainly able to establish [the thesis].
If one were to take "being included among the evolving consciousnesses" as the reason, it would then deviate from the dissimilar class of others. Even if...
Because this nature of consciousness serves as the cause and also functions within its own dissimilar class (*vijātīya*), it cannot avoid the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
[This concludes] the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* establishes an inference (*anumāna*) stating: "The eighth consciousness must necessarily have a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because it is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*), just like the six [sensory] consciousnesses.
This reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), due to the objection that there are [other factors] such as [the homogeneous cause].
That is to say, there is a formal proposition: "The eighth [consciousness] necessarily lacks a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because it is fundamental, just like *tathatā* (suchness).

If one argues that this [proposition] incurs the fault of contradicting the specific characteristics of existing phenomena (*dharmas*)—on the grounds that the eighth consciousness is established as being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—then the aforementioned reason (*hetu*) would likewise incur that same fault, as it establishes the eighth [consciousness].

Eighth, because it is a transforming consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). If one were to say that [the objection] is not established because [the ālayavijñāna] is self[-arising], that too is not a valid objection, as it contradicts its own [tenets].

Now, we establish a distinction: the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas* must necessarily lack a simultaneous objective support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because they are not subsumed under the nature of the six consciousnesses, just like the eye-faculty and so forth. If...

To challenge this reason [that mental factors are not of the nature of cognition], one might argue that there is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*), since it establishes that seven or eight [mental factors] lack the nature of being a cognizer (*ālambaka*), just like the eye-faculty and so forth;
however, this is not the case. This is because mental factors are established as being indeterminate (*anaikāntika*).

If one says that even in relation to the preceding [reasons] there is indeterminacy, because mental factors are not of the nature of the six consciousnesses since they possess a support (*āśraya*), [we reply: this is not so.
This is not indeterminate, because it is based on the sense-faculties (indriya) as the support for the previously established statement.

If one considers them in relation to mental factors (caitta), they are merely supports (āśraya) and not sense-faculties, because they are subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and do not depend upon faculties.

Therefore, although that school recognizes the distinction between the support (niśraya) and the supported (āśrita), they have not yet understood the distinction between the support and the sense-faculty.
This is different. If one discusses the basis (*āśraya*), it extends to all eight consciousnesses as well as their mental factors (*caitta*).

However, the sense organs that serve as its support do not extend to the mental factors, nor to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. There is one who refutes this school by establishing a formal inference (*prayoga*) which states:
"The root co-existent with the mental consciousness is certainly not of the nature of a cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), because it is the object of the six consciousnesses and their mental factors."

Because it is not included [in the aggregates]. Since the six consciousnesses are all included within the single category of the faculties (*indriya*) and their concomitants—just as the eye-faculty and so forth—their school conversely takes the form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) as the "mind" (*manas*), and thus raises this objection.

This critique generally refutes the various schools of the Mahāyāna; however, a fallacy of "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) arises. That is to say, they establish: [The argument: "That which is the object of the six consciousnesses is not the mind, because it is not included in the [five] aggregates, like the eye-faculty. [The Mahāyānist response:

"That which is the object of the six consciousnesses is the mind, because it is included in the sphere of mental objects, like the form-phenomena included therein. Since both arguments are equally valid yet lead to contradictory conclusions, the fallacy of "contradictory certainty" occurs. Thus, they establish...

The mental faculty (manas) is certainly not of the nature of matter (rūpa), because it is the uncommon support for conceptualizing consciousness (savikalpaka-vijñāna), just as attention (manaskāra) is co-existent with the sixth consciousness.

By such arguments, the reason [proposed by the opponent] is shown to be inconclusive (anaikāntika). [The Five Means of Valid Cognition (pramāṇa): 1. Direct perception (pratyakṣa) 2. Inference (anumāna) 3. Scriptural authority (āgama) 4. Analogy (upamāna) 5. Presumption (arthāpatti)

Eleventh: For example, when a teacher of the Śabdika school establishes that sound is permanent because it possesses the nature of being audible, this reason is "contradictory and decisive" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) in relation to the Vaiśeṣika, and "inconclusive and non-common" (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) in relation to the Buddhist disciples, because there is no commonly accepted property in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Someone might raise an objection, stating a formal inference (*prayoga*) to claim that the reason "because of the nature of being audible" should not be [considered valid].
The reason for doubt is that it is absent from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), just like a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*).
Furthermore, this reason should not be considered "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), because it is absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), just like a valid reason (*saddhetu*).
Master Bei stated: "The *Nyāyamukha* says 'because it is exclusively excluded,' which addresses that objection. That is to say, regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*)..."
The nature of hearing is categorized as "inconclusive" because it is invariably dissociated [from the object], just like the "common inconclusive" [reason].

This is because being invariably dissociated from speech lacks one of the necessary characteristics [of a valid reason]. The judgment states: this reason suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive;
for although the nature of what is perceived lacks one characteristic, it is not inconclusive, and thus [the reason] is unestablished. That is to say, [the proponent] establishes...

"Sound is impermanent because it has the nature of being perceived. This reason (hetu) is present in similar instances (sapakṣa) and absent in dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), yet it lacks only the first characteristic [of a valid reason].
Therefore, it is also considered to be deficient in one characteristic.

If, in order to avoid this fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika), one were to formulate the reason differently, it would still lack one of the two remaining characteristics, just as in the case of the four types of reasons, such as the "common" (sādhāraṇa) and so forth.
Regarding the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*): this reason also possesses other instances of inconclusiveness.
For example, in the Madhyamaka school, the reason "because it is dependently originated" lacks one of the two [required] characteristics;

nevertheless, it is a valid reason and not inconclusive, and thus it cannot constitute a contradictory certainty (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). Furthermore, there is no [counter-example] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) as previously established.
Therefore, that which is not a cause of doubt is also non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), such as the various contradictory and equally valid reasons (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

Although these do not exist in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), they are causes of doubt; thus, only a reason that is absent from the similar class (*sapakṣa*) can be established as not being a cause of doubt by way of avoiding the inconclusive.
In this regard, one should formulate a formal inference (*sādharmya-prayoga*) based on contradiction.
This means that the nature of what is heard is subsumed under the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), because it establishes contradictory theses (*viruddha-pakṣa*).
It is just like a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika-hetu*). As the *Nyāyamukha* clarifies regarding this reason:

"If one establishes all specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*) as being universally pervasive (*vyāpta*) within the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that is not [otherwise] unique (*asādhāraṇa*), these are all reasons for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*)."
It is because that [property] exists only in that [subject] and is subsumed by it, and because it is invariably excluded [from others].

According to this analysis, regarding what is established as non-common: for example, establishing that sound is permanent because it possesses the property of being audible, or establishing that it is impermanent because it possesses the property of being audible;
in all such cases, there is no [reason] that is not established equally [for both sides]. Therefore, it is said that "whatever exists is universally subsumed."
All [of these] are, by this principle, causes for doubt when compared to that "nature of what is heard" (*śruta-dharmatā*), because they are entirely excluded from it.
The phrase "because they are entirely excluded" refers to the meaning of establishing various tenets through transformation and so forth.
This is because, when compared to those tenets, they are both common and uncommon; "common" has the sense of being "entirely" (*ekānta*), while "uncommon" is the sense of being "excluded."

Regarding the meaning: because it is invariably excluded [from the subject] and because it establishes various contradictory positions equally, its reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). (The fifth proof.)
Regarding the establishment of two types of inference based on the contradiction of the twelve [fallacies], Master Wengu composed his own questions and answers.
Question: Since that which possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) should be a correct reason (*saddhetu*), why is it said here that this is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*)?
Answer: This doubt remains unresolved, and I do not dare to explain it.
There is one who provides a general interpretation, following along to provide a commentary on the intent of the question herein, establishing an inference (*anumāna*) as follows:

"The reason that contradicts the definitive resolution must be a valid reason (*saddhetu*), because it possesses the three characteristics (*trairūpya*), just like any other true reason. Now, the general interpretation states: "It contradicts the definitive resolution..."
These two reasons are not subsumed under "valid reasons" (*saddhetu*), because they are subject to the same difficulties as the "contradictory reason" (*viruddhahetu*).

By this, it is shown that they possess the fallacy of being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, these two reasons are not subsumed under "contradictory reasons," because they exist within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), just like a valid reason.
Moreover, these two reasons are not subsumed under "unestablished reasons" (*asiddha*), as they are commonly accepted.
Therefore, just as with the *asādhāraṇa-hetu* (uncommon reason), these two reasons are subsumed under the category of *anaikāntika-hetu* (inconclusive reasons).

This is because they are neither contradictory (*viruddha*), nor non-establishment (*asiddha*). They are like the other five types of inconclusive reasons. [Sixth: The Means of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa*).]

Thirteenth: Or, regarding the fivefold nature [of those who lack the potential], one might establish a formal inference (*anumāna*) stating that sentient beings without the [Buddha-]nature must certainly attain Buddhahood, because they possess a mind, just like those who possess the nature.
This reason is not definitive; therefore, it does not constitute a valid objection. For instance, just as with the Buddhas, although they possess a mind, they are not [yet] to [attain Buddhahood].
"Will they become Buddhas? Like Bodhisattvas, because they possess a mind [set on enlightenment], they must necessarily become Buddhas.

The reason previously established—that "because they are sentient beings who have not yet attained Buddhahood"—is also subject to the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to other possibilities.
Is it like those of the Bodhisattva lineage, or is it like those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who are fixed in their destiny? If...
To avoid this [fallacy], another thesis is established: "Sentient beings who lack the nature [of Buddhahood] are determined;
those of the two vehicles shall all become Buddhas. This is because they are included among sentient beings who have not yet attained Buddhahood, just like Bodhisattvas.
Since there are such objections, [the original reason] becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, these three types of persons are not destined to become Buddhas, because...
Because there are no untainted seeds of the Mahāyāna that are not subsumed within the bodhisattva lineage, [the opponent's position] would be like insentient things such as wood or stone.
Furthermore, it entails the fault of contradicting inference (*anumāna-virodha*):
namely, when the other four of the five lineages fall into hell, they should possess four qualities, as you yourself admit.
If [you claim] the Buddha is therefore [not omniscient], it is like the lineage of a bodhisattva. To grant this contradicts the teachings; to deny it contradicts reason.
This is the fault of contradicting the inference based on one’s own realization (*svasaṃvedana-anumāna*). [Thus ends the discussion of] the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, in order to refute [the existence of] the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), he establishes a formal inference (*prayoga*) as follows:
"All instances of the view of a self do not take a real self as their object, because they possess an objective referent (*ālambana*), just like other cognitions.
The object of the view of a self is certainly not a real self, because it is an objective referent, just like other phenomena. Furthermore, he says:

The various phenomena grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles are not substantially existent entities distinct from mind and mental factors, because they are objects of apprehension, just like mind and mental factors themselves;
thus, the cognition that apprehends them does not take them as its object either.

Because this is a grasper (*grāhaka*), it is like the cognition that takes this as its object. It is judged that there are four types of inference (*anumāna*) herein, which constitute true refutations (*bhaṅga*).

They refute both the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), and because no fault arises [in their application], they are valid. Alternatively, based on these refutations, one may refute the Mahāyāna by stating:
"The cognitions of the aspect of the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭamavijñāna*) do not take the *ālayavijñāna* as their objective aspect (*nimitta*)."

Because there is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), the principle of proof through reasoning (*upapattisādhanayukti*) is extremely difficult to conceive. Were it not for this, it would be easily understood as a mere joke;
now, relying on the sacred scriptures, I shall present one corner [of the teaching]. May it flow through the Buddha-way throughout the three periods of time.
*Pian bilian lun* (Treatise on Determining Inference), one fascicle. Composed by Śramaṇa Yuanxiao.
On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Xianheng era, the year of Xinwei, the writing was completed at Zhuxing Temple.
Recorded by Zu.

Regarding the newly discovered fragmentary manuscripts, what they state consists of two points: similarity and dissimilarity. To claim that while their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are contradictory, the essence (*svabhāva*) of the word is one, is certainly unreasonable.
It is judged that there are nine types of inference (*anumāna*) herein; among them, the first six refute the opponent's position.
In our own school, the latter three types of valid cognition refute Saṃghabhadra’s defense as follows:
[First,] at the time of conjunction, the eye and so forth should not be distinct from the preceding eye and so forth, because they are [merely] the same as color, sound, and so on;

[Second,] by analogy, they should not be identical, because the entity of "sameness" and "difference" cannot be one and the same, just as the characteristic of difference is not identical with its locus; [Third,] therefore, by analogy, they are like the distant [object] of the same class.
This is not reasonable because it contradicts one's own inference (*svārthānumāna*). In this context, some might refute the Mahāyāna by saying:

"The Mahāyāna’s form-base (*rūpāyatana*) must not be a conventional form (*prajñaptirūpa*), because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), just like the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) and so forth; the same applies to other bases.
If the Mahāyāna school were to admit the existence of conventional form, then it could not avoid such faults as these. However, this Mahāyāna...
It is not permitted to assert that there are real forms (rūpa) based on the claim that there are merely conventional forms;

for if one were to do so, their own proofs would be established as already proven, since all categories of phenomena—such as the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)—are merely conventional designations established upon words. (The tenth proof.)
The *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*: Colophon The principles of proof are exceedingly difficult to conceive; were it not for this [work], they would be hard to understand even for those of subtle intellect.
Now, relying upon the sacred scriptures, I shall provide an illustration of one corner [of the subject]. May [this work] circulate through the Buddha-way throughout the three periods of time.
A Commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa* in One Fascicle. Composed by Wonhyo.
On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Hwangheung era, the year of Sin-mi (1671), this was written at the Janghaengmyeong-sa Temple and completed.
